blocks.text: 18 January 2023
Baby G +Baby H: Parents' statements + Kate Tyndall (Police Analyst)
CONTENTS
DR DEWI EVANS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Questions from THE JUDGE
DR SANDIE BOHIN (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Summary of interview with LUCY Letby re [Baby G] (read)

Wednesday, 18 January 2023
(In the absence of the jury)

Mr Johnson, it has been a long time since the court sat on this trial and it may be helpful, just before you resume calling the evidence -- and I thank you or Mr Driver for the witness list, I anticipated it would have been amended from last week's to the format for this week -- just very briefly to remind the jury as to what this evidence is going to go to, which counts, just because it is a number of -- you're prepared for that? Good, I thought you would be.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)

Good morning, members of the jury. We've had a slightly longer break than the long break that we were going to have had in any event for the Christmas holiday period. We're going to resume now with the evidence and pick up where we left off before Christmas. Mr Johnson is just going to remind you of the context of where we are, I'm sure you remember. It is [Baby G] and it is
in relation to the two counts -- there were three counts of alleged attempted murder. We are now going to deal with the second and third counts. That's right, Mr Johnson, isn't it?
It is, my Lord. It may help you, ladies and gentlemen -- and it's an exercise I did myself, really, just to recalibrate my own thoughts -- just to go to the indictment if you would, page 3.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Bundle 1, divider 1, page 3. You'll remember that there are three counts relating to [Baby G]. They are counts 7, 8 and 9. Insofar as count 7 was concerned, we'd concluded all that evidence. That was the projectile vomiting that ended up on the floor and on the chair next to the cot, you'll remember, on 7 September 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The evidence that we heard in the week before the break concerned counts 8 and 9, which are two events on the same day. The first, count 8, was at 10.15 on the morning of the 21st, so exactly 2 weeks after count 7; that concerns projectile vomiting again. And count 9 was an incident where [Baby G] desaturated where she had been detached from the monitor and the monitor was switched off. I'm sure you remember that and you will remember Dr Gibbs, Dr Harkness, [Nurse B] and others telling you about that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What we're about to do is to call Doctors Evans and Bohin to deal with counts 8 and 9. They have, of course, already dealt with count 7. I say "and count 9": they don't deal at all with count 9, that's a factual issue as to what was going on from the witness evidence. So far as Doctors Bohin and Evans are concerned, their evidence is limited to the vomiting and desaturation that's represented by count 8.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And just to help you to put yourself back into what you were thinking just before we finished for the break, when Dr Evans comes in I'll probably spend about 2 or 3 minutes running through the chronology of [Baby G] from birth to the events of the 7th and then the 21 September, just to remind you of the key dates.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We are not going to go over all the evidence again. It just may be helpful just to put you back into the way you were thinking and what you were thinking a month ago. All right? So Dr Evans, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR DEWI EVANS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Welcome back, Dr Evans. For the record would you identify yourself, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Dewi Evans.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you, doctor. You have already told the jury that you have written several reports relating to [Baby G]; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And so far as the incidents of 21 September 2015 are concerned, you address those first in your report of 24 March 2019 --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that is correct. That is something I had overlooked in my first report.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Well, I'll come to that in a second, but can we just go back to your -- just to set the scene, as it were, and to remind the jury of [Baby G]'s progress. Can we look at your report of 31 May, please, 2018?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So far as that report was concerned, that followed your initial sift report, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Which was compiled, like so many others, in the latter part of 2017?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If you wouldn't mind, please, could you go to page 3 of 16 of your report of 31 May 2018. There you deal with [Baby G]'s clinical progress; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your paragraph 6 makes it clear that she was born on 31 May 2015.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: She was of very, very low weight at birth, 535 grams.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And she had been born at Arrowe Park Hospital, which of course we know is a tertiary centre.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There then followed a prolonged course of treatment at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Which included a transfer to Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool, where what's called a Broviac line was inserted to administer medication and feed; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And [Baby G] was transferred from Arrowe Park to the Countess of Chester Hospital on 13 August 2015.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You reviewed her treatment from 14 August through to 7 September -- and 7 September, of course, was the occasion on which [Baby G] produced a projectile vomit, which got as far as the chair next to her cot --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- and also the floor. And 45ml of feed was removed from her stomach after the vomiting.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you've already given us evidence about your views so far as that is concerned.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'd like to turn, if we may, then, to your report of 24 March 2019. So this was the third of your reports; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: At your paragraph 5 onwards, did you conduct a further review of the clinical data relating to [Baby G]'s stay at Chester?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you note what you describe as a significant event on 21 September 2015 which in your previous two reports you had not addressed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just to give the jury some sort of idea of what you were dealing with, at paragraph 3 of that report, so just going back to page 2, you refer to the volume of material that you had received concerning [Baby G]'s treatment.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: How many pages of material were there relating to this single child?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just over 4,000.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. All right. So there you were in March of 2019 conducting a further review. I'm looking at your paragraph 6 now, Dr Evans. What did you note?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, having looked at it again, I found another event, as we already mentioned, on 21 September, and this is -- this occurred during the morning, around 10 o'clock in the morning, on 21 September, when she had what were described as two further projectile vomits. These were witnessed by nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, a projectile vomit is where the baby vomits far beyond its body size, so therefore these were very significant vomits and, even more worryingly and more significantly, her oxygen saturation dropped and it dropped to 30%.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, normal saturation is over 90%, so an oxygen saturation of 30 is very, very low and is life-threatening. In other words, you've got to get the oxygen level back to normal as soon as possible.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that is what happened on the morning.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Because it's a month since we heard this evidence, if Mr Murphy would help us, please, can we go to tile 50 first of all.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is the note written by Lucy Letby relating to an event that she recorded as having occurred at 10.15.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we can just remind ourselves of what she wrote, please. The note says at 10.15:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Times] 2 large projectile milky vomits. Brief self-resolving apnoea and desaturation to 35% with colour loss."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Top right there. Top left, sorry.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Top left, yes. So if we just go above that slightly, Mr Murphy, to take in the line above where it says:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "NG tube feed. EBM [expressed breast milk] given..."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Presumably that should say "at 9 o'clock" as [Baby G] was feeding (inaudible: coughing).
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then where the arrow is:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "10.15 x2 large projectile milky vomits. Brief self-resolving apnoea. Desaturation to 35% with colour loss. NG tube aspirated: 30ml undigested milk discarded. Abdomen distended, soft. Doctors asked to review. Temperatures remain low. Tachycardic over 180 beats per minute. Mum states that [Baby G] doesn't appear as well as she did yesterday."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we could just move on to put this into overall context to the next tile, please, Mr Murphy, and to the record of Dr Fielding.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We'll work off the analyst's typed transcription of the handwritten notes. We can see it says:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Baby G] had episode at about 10.20 where she had 2x projectile vomits witnessed by nursing staff, after which she was apnoeic for about 6 to 10 seconds. Went blue. Saturations decreased to 30%. Last feed 9 am.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurse called for help. On going back to [Baby G], colour..."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is that "normal"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "... breathing plus crying."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So is that the material that you were referring to?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. So that's your paragraph 6, Dr Evans. Did you also in your report refer to other material from that particular date and events which had been recorded?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The important bit is that the examination of [Baby G] showed that the abdomen was distended, in other words the abdomen was larger than it should be, and that her bowel sounds
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: were active. Now, bowel sounds active means that the intestinal system was working perfectly well, but the abdomen was distended, which would occur if the abdomen was either full of milk or full of air or full of a combination of milk and air. So that's the pattern that occurred here and that occurred despite her having vomited, because by vomiting, of course, you'd expect any abdominal distension to reduce because some of the substance in the stomach had been vomited up.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So in other words, this was a very significant concerning issue, particularly in relation to -- particularly in association with the oxygen saturation dropping to 30% and that she went blue and she also stopped breathing for a few seconds.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So a concerning event.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. So what did you -- going to your opinion section, your paragraph 18 onwards, what conclusions did you draw from your review of all those circumstances?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. Well, I thought that, generally speaking, she'd had a potentially life-threatening episode of vomiting and oxygen desaturation. That was my overall impression and that there was one explanation for this, which is that [Baby G] had been given far more milk during her nasogastric tube feed an hour earlier. The plan was to give her 40ml of milk and she had been tolerating that amount of milk by bottle the previous day, 40ml or 45ml, so therefore if you -- if she had been given 40ml of milk then it would not explain how she had two large vomits, two large projectile vomits, and on top of that there were still 30ml of milk left in her stomach.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore my conclusion was that she had not received 40ml of milk, she had received a lot more than that, and it was the excessive amount of milk that she had received had caused this episode at 10 o'clock on 21 September.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you limit your opinion to the substance being inserted into [Baby G] being restricted to milk?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, it could have been milk or it could have been milk and air. And there's no way of saying how much milk and how much air. Of course, you do not vomit air, you can only vomit a liquid, and therefore there was -- clearly a large amount of milk, over and above 40ml, had been given to the little babe, which is what caused her vomiting in the first place.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you, Dr Evans. Would you wait there, please, for some further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Evans, just with regard to when this appears in the reports that you produced, we know you provided an initial report on [Baby G] on 16 November, didn't you --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: 6 November, actually.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Sorry, 6 November 2017. And then you provided a second report on 31 May 2018.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And as you've just explained to us, this incident on the 21st was identified by you in your third report on 24 March 2019?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The nursing notes are items that were provided to you from when you first began to consider the case, weren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your view when you wrote the report, your second report, on 31 May 2018 -- bear with me one moment, please...
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)
I'm looking at paragraph 27. Just to assist the jury whilst you turn that up, these first two reports both focused on the incident on 7 September, the first incident?
Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And in the second report, having looked at the material, you said this at the end of paragraph 27:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I scrutinised these entries [this is the rest of the clinical entries]. They record reasonable progress.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have not found any evidence of any acute life-threatening event."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what you said, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now you did say that at a time when you had been able to read these nursing notes, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not really. What I did initially -- if we recall, I prepared about 30 reports which were done towards the end of 2017 and I concentrated -- 30 reports is a lot of reports and they were sift reports, as we've heard. And this case had 4,000 pages plus. That's about eight of these folders (indicating). And quite frankly, the event of 21 September, I overlooked it, didn't see it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And I didn't see it because I concentrated my review on the medical notes more than the nursing notes. So I overlooked it, simple as that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: When you did make reference to this event in your third report, the one dated 24 March 2019, you also identified the 30 September as a date that required further consideration, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What you said at paragraph 20 was:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "There is a need to review the nursing and medical staffing present at the intensive care unit during the hours leading up to the events of 30 September 2015."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just so the jury can see what it is that had caught your attention then, I'm going to ask Mr Murphy, if he would, please, to put J7425 on the screens. Ladies and gentlemen, this isn't in the sequence of events, it's something additional, but it relates to this period.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we go to the right-hand side of page 7425 -- we're there, aren't we? -- this is the section. When you did the report in which you identified 21 September, you also identified this, didn't you, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And what had caught your attention was this: we can see it's 30 September, at 17.04, an entry by MT, who we know is Melanie Taylor and what we have is as we go down:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Bottle fed [halfway down the report]. SVIA at start shift."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that self-ventilating in air?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "Having a few desats. Informed doctors before handover due to..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that immunisations, "imms"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think so, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "1x profound saturation apnoea requiring position changed and oxygen this morning. Bottle fed very well this morning. Observations within satisfactory limits, no increased work of breathing. ROP this afternoon."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not sure what ROP means. Can you help us?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think it's retinopathy of prematurity examination maybe. Maybe. I'm not sure actually.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It moves on:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Dr Butcher does not need follow-up ROP screen. Has updated mum. Very sleepy after ROP. Increased desats so put onto nasal prong oxygen."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So that was something additional that you thought required further consideration; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. We can take that down, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: With regard to the incident on 21 September, Dr Evans, particular points about that, it's described as projectile vomiting in the notes, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And it's that in particular that you have identified as a cause for concern, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We don't have on this occasion any indication of the extent or distance of the vomit, do we? You didn't have that to work with like you did on the 7th?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The event itself on the 21st, the one we're talking about today, does appear to have been a relatively brief and selfresolving event, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I wouldn't call it self-resolving. They had to address the issue, her stomach was aspirated, the doctors were called. She was quite unwell during this period of time. So it wasn't one of these self-limiting desaturations, it was much worse than that. And of course, the key thing was that she actually vomited two large vomits.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It was brief, wasn't it, relatively brief?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it wasn't. You see, the only thing that was brief was that she stopped breathing for 6 to 10 seconds.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, 6 to 10 seconds might not sound a lot but this was a baby by this time who was over 2 kilos and had been feeding by bottle the day before. So this was quite a serious event. I don't think it was as serious an event as the one we discussed before Christmas, but it was a significant event.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Dr Fielding, whose notes we've just been to, and whose evidence we heard on 14 December 2022, was the doctor who came and attended to [Baby G] on this occasion, wasn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just so we can keep the evidence in mind because it's a while ago, he was asked that this had been a brief episode and there had been a relatively swift recovery, his answer to that was yes, Dr Evans --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I heard that. As I've said, I don't think this was as serious an event as the earlier one, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The air. You've mentioned air in the bowel or in the Xrays; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's a feature, isn't it, of [Baby G] throughout her stay in whichever hospital she was in that there were multiple occasions when there was air in her intestines or bowels over the months of treatment?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Dr Fielding also described -- we can put up tile 51, please, Mr Murphy. Can we go into the tile, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you want to go to the document behind it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Please. Could we go to the notes, please, Mr Murphy? My fault.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I've tried to do it on the iPad and it says it can't find the PDF. Are you the same?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I can assist. We have seen this before, so I can simply read what it is that I wanted to refer to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Fielding recorded that [Baby G] passed a loose green stool about 10 minutes after the vomit.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you agree, Dr Evans, that it is possible that a loose stool -- thank you, here we have it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It might in fact be over the page, please, if we can go over the page after all of that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Towards the bottom of that page, there's a reference to the episode.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. The reference I wish to make, I'm not sure it follows this or not, it's something he referred to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Is there a page that follows this, Mr Murphy? If we go down to the lower half of that page, we can see it says:
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "Bowels open. Loose stool. Green colour."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you accept there are circumstances where that may indicate some poor health or some indication of becoming unwell?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Difficult to say just with one. Right. There are a few things this tells me. First of all, it tells me there's no intestinal obstruction. In other words, the vomiting is not due to some blockage because everything is going through and some of it is coming out the other end, so we can be sure of that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: One loose stool... loose stool. Babies have loose stools, you know.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If we move, please, to tile 58 then, just following on.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just the pathology sample. We can go into this.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just look at the CRP, which is in the centre of the page. We understand a little bit about CRP, as we all do, Dr Evans, you may know a great deal more, but that is C-reactive protein, which can be a marker of infection potentially?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It is raised slightly at this point, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's over 10, so it's 18, so it's marginally raised, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you for those, Mr Murphy. Thank you, Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: With regard to the vomiting, do you agree that once [Baby G] returned to the Countess of Chester from Arrowe Park there was a more marked history of vomiting from that point onwards?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, there's a huge change to [Baby G]'s overall health following the event of 7 September. And this relates to the abnormalities found on MRI I think carried out on 15 September from memory. The brain scans carried out at Arrowe Park did not show any significant abnormalities and I think we had the report from the neuroradiologist, so her brain scans prior to 7 September were satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Her MRI of the 15th showed very significant abnormalities. And therefore from 7 September onwards, [Baby G] was a completely different baby from a developmental point of view.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's the events of 7 September that changed her significantly from a neurological point of view, in other words from the brain development point of view, and so, yes -- and I think -- well, we now know that [Baby G] receives feeding by tube. So in other words, vomiting has been a significant part of her life from mid-September.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right. In your third report, paragraphs 13 and 14, you list some of the occasions from the notes in which vomiting features in the records that are kept of her at the Countess of Chester, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We may see a little of this later. There are numerous events after her return to the Countess of Chester on 16 September when she is recorded as vomiting, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And therefore, whilst there is the vomiting on the 21st that you identify, conceivably that could be part of a pattern of vomiting which has continued thereafter as a result of earlier events?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I disagree with that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The reason I disagree with that is to do with basic arithmetic. In other words, I'm sure that she had more milk than she should have on the 21st. The reason for that is basic arithmetic. If she had had 40ml in there was no way that she would have vomited -- had two projectile vomits, sorry, two large vomits, and there was still 30ml still left in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In her interview on 5 July 2018, Lucy Letby remembered [Baby G] and was taken through the relevant notes. She recalled that
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Nurse E] was [Baby G]'s designated nurse on 7 September 2015, there were no clinical concerns at the start of the shift, and Lucy Letby agreed that the notes suggested that she took over care at 2 am but she couldn't recall why she'd taken over [Baby G]'s care.

blocks.text: Lucy Letby had found [Baby G] vomiting and confirmed that it was projectile vomiting of a large volume of milky-coloured vomit. blocks.text: "Sometimes when babies vomit, they can take on air as well if they're gasping with the vomiting."

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was asked to recall how long it had taken for [Baby G] to desaturate following the doctor being called away and Lucy Letby could not recall. blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In respect of the events of 21 September 2015, Lucy Letby had a vague recollection of the shift. She'd looked after [Baby G] as her designated nurse in nursery 4 for a period of time that
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: morning. blocks.text: Witness statement of [MOTHER OF BABY H] (read)
17 October 2017. Members of the jury, it reads:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am making this statement in regards to my daughter, [Baby H], and her time at the Countess of Chester Hospital, more specifically the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I currently reside with my husband, [Father of Baby H], and our only child [Baby H], who was born on 22 September 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I discovered that I was expecting [Baby H] in February 2015. Mike and I had been trying for a baby and, as such, it was a planned pregnancy. [Baby H] was conceived naturally. I had, to all intents and purposes, a healthy pregnancy. The only real complication was that I am a type 1 diabetic. This required extra scans and additional trips to the hospital for regular checks, although this was primarily to check on my health as opposed to concern about [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I went into the Countess of Chester Hospital on Sunday, 20 September 2015, primarily because my blood sugar level kept dropping and I couldn't get control over it by my usual methods. I contacted the hospital and they asked me to attend, which I did.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "This was initially only so they could monitor me and try and get my blood sugar under control. Once there, they started to talk about the possibility of inducing me if there was no improvement in my blood sugar after a couple of days. I was therefore admitted to hospital and given a course of steroids.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At this stage I was 34 weeks and 3 days pregnant.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It was evening time when I went into hospital and I spent that night and all of Monday daytime under observation, still with the view that I wouldn't be giving birth for a few weeks.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "This changed on Tuesday morning when I was visited by the consultant, who told me that it had been decided that it would be best for both [Baby H] and I that she should be delivered that day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The consultant wanted to go ahead as soon as possible. However, there was an issue because [Baby H] was going to be a couple of weeks premature and she might need to go into the NNU. There were, however, no beds available in the Countess' NNU, so calls were being made to other hospitals to try and find one that was available. Apparently, there were no other beds available in the local area even with them checking as far away as Birmingham.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It got to about 6 pm on the Tuesday and the staff informed me that they could not wait any longer and we were going to theatre to deliver [Baby H]. It was only at that moment that a doctor from the NNU appeared and announced that a bed had just become available within the NNU. Consequently, I went to theatre and [Baby H] was born without issue at just under 6 weeks premature.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Immediately after, the doctor examined her and informed me that she was absolutely fine and may not even need to go to the NNU. In fact, she had an Apgar score of 9 and a weight of 5 pounds and 2 ounces. Both Mike and I were allowed to hold her. However, she began to look pale and make grunting noises when breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was taken for a more thorough examination by a neonatal doctor who had arrived at the theatre. He explained that [Baby H] was going to be taken to the NNU so she could be put on to oxygen as she was apparently struggling to breathe.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby H] was then taken to the NNU. I had to remain in the maternity unit for a short while. Mike and my mother went with [Baby H]. Later that night, I had been told that if I could get out of bed I could go and see [Baby H]. I got up and moved to a wheelchair and was assisted to the NNU by a nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When I arrived, I met a NNU nurse called Kate.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Kate explained why [Baby H] was there and what they were doing for her. She explained that [Baby H] seemed to be struggling for air and, as a result, was on oxygen only.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: However, after a short while, it was necessary to put her on a CPAP machine to further assist with her breathing.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The following morning, I was not permitted to go and see [Baby H] by myself and there was no one available on the ward to assist with getting me there. Therefore I had to await Mike's arrival. As soon as he did arrive, we both went to the NNU. On arrival, we were stopped by staff as we tried to go in to see [Baby H] and informed that overnight she'd been placed on a ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We were both quite annoyed that no one had let us know and expressed this. Staff explained that their first priority had been to care for [Baby H], implying that they had not had time to inform us. We accepted that to a certain extent, but reinforced what a shock it had been to arrive at the NNU and find [Baby H] on a ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Due to her being ventilated and more unstable, we were no longer able to pick [Baby H] up. After several X-rays it was explained that [Baby H] had possibly suffered a lung puncture, which is why she had needed to go on to the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We remained with [Baby H] for the whole day. She was in an incubator, ventilated, so we had no physical contact with her. Numerous staff members came and went, performing multiple minor tests and medical procedures.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We stayed with [Baby H] until quite late, probably about 11 pm, at which point staff told me I really needed to go and get some sleep, so I returned to the maternity ward and Mike went home.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At some point in the early hours of the morning some nurses from the NNU and the maternity unit came into my room and told me I had to come to the NNU right away. I followed them from the maternity, I was also told to call Mike and tell him to come to the hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: They were actually running along the corridors.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I remember that we took a short cut around the back of the maternity unit. I was trying to ask questions but they just kept saying I needed to come now.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I arrived at the entrance to the room where [Baby H] was being treated. There were lots of medical personnel around [Baby H]. Most of the ventilator equipment had been removed from her face
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: and the lid to her incubator was open. It was obvious to me that they were resuscitating her.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "They told me to go into the room and just sit with her and hold her hand, which I did. Mike also arrived at this time. The staff managed to get [Baby H] back and then continued working on her, including putting a new chest drain into her.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "They were not able to explain why she had suffered a cardiac collapse. The staff told us that [Baby H] was recovering well and that they did not anticipate any further problems.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Throughout that day [Baby H] seemed to pick up and was apparently doing really well. The hospital managed to free up a room. We stayed with [Baby H] until about 11 pm before going to sleep in the room provided. Mike and I had just gone to bed when there was a knock on the door. Staff came into the room and told us we were needed back with [Baby H] as she was not responding.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was surprised as she had been fine when we had gone to bed. However, we were met with an almost identical scene to the previous occasion with multiple medical staff working on [Baby H] inside her incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Fortunately, she was not in a collapse as long this time and it took less time to stabilise her. A short while after this second collapse and resuscitation, a consultant from Arrowe Park attended via ambulance and they began preparing to transfer [Baby H] to that hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This was at around 6 am on Sunday, 27 September.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Consequently, we arrived at Arrowe Park on Sunday.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: They examined [Baby H] and the first thing they did was to remove the ventilator and then reapply it to their satisfaction. Arrowe Park did numerous tests on [Baby H] to try and establish what had caused her collapses.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: They looked closely at her heart and also gave her a brain scan, which, fortunately, showed she had suffered no long-term damage.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "It was clear to us that [Baby H] improved dramatically almost as soon as she arrived at Arrowe Park. There were no further collapses. While at Chester, [Baby H]'s monitors regularly set off alarms and doctors had to attend and clear her airways. This didn't happen at all at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Within 24 hours [Baby H] was off her ventilator and back on to a CPAP machine. This also was only for 24 hours, by which time she had recovered to such an extent that she was sent back to
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Chester. I would say she was like a completely different baby once at Arrowe Park.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby H] was only at Arrowe Park for 2 days. She made a dramatic improvement and was transferred back to the Countess. On our return, [Baby H] was initially placed in the intensive care area of the NNU. By this stage the only real concern was that we were having a bit of difficulty getting her to feed.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Consequently, we were only in the intensive care area for a brief period of time before moving on to one of the side nursery areas where she stayed for a couple of nights before moving to the final nursery room, where she was able to sleep normally in a regular cot with no machines or other assistance.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "After a period of 18 days, [Baby H] was finally discharged from hospital on 9 October 2015. She had several more scans and tests but has been absolutely fine and healthy ever since. In fact, she was discharged earlier than normal for a premature baby outpatient. There have been no long-term health issues or complications whatsoever."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That concludes the relevant part of [Mother of Baby H]'s statement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of [FATHER OF BABY H] (read)
Turning to a statement made by her husband [Father of Baby H], dated 4 May 2020, he introduces their domestic situation and then says:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby H] was born on 22 September 2015 and I have been asked about her birth and her stay in the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was born on a Tuesday and they did their checks and said she was quite healthy and she had quite a high Apgar score. She was grimacing and had some complications with her breathing and so was taken into the NNU, which is where she stayed. Having been taken away, [Mother of Baby H] wasn't able to see her straightaway but I was able to visit her shortly afterwards in nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was in an incubator and was on CPAP to help her breathe. So we spent time in there from Tuesday onwards and on the Friday. I had been there late with [Mother of Baby H]'s mum on Friday until about midnight and we'd come back to the house.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was awoken by her in the early hours. She'd had a call from [Mother of Baby H] that we needed to go back to the hospital. We drove back there and I just remember looking down into the ward,
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: into the high dependency unit, and seeing a lot of commotion going on. I can't remember who the designated nurse was that night, but I definitely remember Lucy being there as she was doing the chest massaging.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There was also a nurse there who was about to leave the unit to move to Australia and a nurse called Nicky.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We got into the area and it was explained to us that [Baby H] had had a collapse. I can't remember the exact term that was used. Dr Ravi came in and put some chest drains in her, but prior to that I remember she was getting massaged by Lucy and that she was a very strange colour, very mottled.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "As [Baby H] was coming back round, I remember the mottling was running out of her skin towards her fingers. That was when Dr Gibbs explained that the pressurised air in her lungs had caused a tear, which is why they had had to put chest drains in. He said they couldn't guarantee it wouldn't happen again or that she would make it through the night.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We stayed with her until the early hours of the morning and throughout the next day, which was a Saturday. They then gave us the option to stay with her on the ward to be close to her. She was okay during the Saturday day and then, quite late on, I remember going to the parents' bedroom on the ward to get some sleep. It was only shortly afterwards that we got a knock on the door to say she had deteriorated and she needed medical attention and for us to go and be with her at her bedside. So we went back to her room and there were more doctors and nurses and, I think because of what had happened the previous night, they were in consultation with Arrowe Park Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I vaguely remember them doing X-rays on her to see how the tube was positioned and whether it was touching the vagal nerve or not. After that, in the early hours of Sunday morning, she was transferred to Arrowe Park Hospital. She was only there a few days but she was just like a different baby. She was more responsive and more with it and she just came on in leaps and bounds.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Whereas in Chester it seemed like they were very happy to make slow progress and just keep her stable, in Arrowe Park the doctors were taking chest drains out and being more proactive. It was a completely different set-up. All the babies were in one room with a nursing station looking over them.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Once they were happy she was stable, she went back to Chester. I can't remember who welcomed us back but [Baby H] was in a room with a baby called [Baby G]. We went back into the high dependency room and you had to then work your way through the
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: different rooms before you can go home, so we went through that process and nothing else major really happened.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She went through all the different stages and then I think it was a Friday or Saturday that she got discharged, about a week or so later."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, that concludes the relevant part of [Father of Baby H]'s statement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I hope that's a fair representation.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'd be grateful if Ms Letby could remain for a short while after court because we'd like to speak to her if possible.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I know it was a bad journey this morning, so it will be difficult for everyone who's come from --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We understand.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Mr Myers is going to come down and see you before you go. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Thursday, 19 January 2023)
